questions.question: [New and Emerging Technologies] Explain how 3D printing has changed the prototype development process in product design.
questions.correctAnswer: 3D printing allows designers to create physical prototypes directly from CAD files in hours rather than weeks; it enables iterative testing, reduces material waste compared to subtractive methods, and allows complex geometries that CNC cannot produce.
questions.explanation: 3D printing allows designers to create physical prototypes directly from CAD files in hours rather than weeks; it enables iterative testing, reduces material waste compared to subtractive methods, and allows complex geometries that CNC cannot produce.

questions.question: [New and Emerging Technologies] Discuss the social and economic impacts of increasing automation in manufacturing.
questions.correctAnswer: Positive: increased productivity, consistent quality, reduced hazardous work for humans. Negative: job displacement, skills gap, initial investment costs, dependence on technology. A balanced answer considers both sides with specific examples.
questions.explanation: Positive: increased productivity, consistent quality, reduced hazardous work for humans. Negative: job displacement, skills gap, initial investment costs, dependence on technology. A balanced answer considers both sides with specific examples.

questions.question: [New and Emerging Technologies] Evaluate how the Internet of Things could influence the design of a domestic kettle.
questions.correctAnswer: An IoT kettle could: be controlled remotely via smartphone, learn user habits for energy efficiency, alert users to limescale build-up via sensors, integrate with smart-home energy monitoring. Evaluation should weigh convenience against cost, privacy and reliability concerns.
questions.explanation: An IoT kettle could: be controlled remotely via smartphone, learn user habits for energy efficiency, alert users to limescale build-up via sensors, integrate with smart-home energy monitoring. Evaluation should weigh convenience against cost, privacy and reliability concerns.

questions.question: [Ferrous and Non-Ferrous Metals] Explain why stainless steel is used for surgical instruments whereas mild steel is not, despite both being ferrous metals.
questions.correctAnswer: Stainless steel has 10.5%+ chromium which forms a passive chromium oxide layer - self-healing, prevents rust even when scratched. Mild steel has no chromium and rusts rapidly.
questions.explanation: Stainless steel has 10.5%+ chromium which forms a passive chromium oxide layer - self-healing, prevents rust even when scratched. Mild steel has no chromium and rusts rapidly.

questions.question: [Ferrous and Non-Ferrous Metals] Justify the use of aluminium rather than steel for aircraft fuselage construction.
questions.correctAnswer: Aluminium: density 2.7 g/cm3 vs steel 7.8 - 1/3 the weight, crucial for fuel efficiency; corrosion-resistant; good strength-to-weight when alloyed. Trade-off: more expensive and less stiff.
questions.explanation: Aluminium: density 2.7 g/cm3 vs steel 7.8 - 1/3 the weight, crucial for fuel efficiency; corrosion-resistant; good strength-to-weight when alloyed. Trade-off: more expensive and less stiff.

questions.question: [Ferrous and Non-Ferrous Metals] A product designer needs a gold-coloured, corrosion-resistant material for a door handle. Compare brass and gold-anodised aluminium.
questions.correctAnswer: Brass: genuine gold appearance, naturally corrosion-resistant, heavy and tactile (premium feel), low friction, antimicrobial. Gold-anodised aluminium: lighter, cheaper, coating can scratch to reveal silver beneath. For a door handle: brass is superior.
questions.explanation: Brass: genuine gold appearance, naturally corrosion-resistant, heavy and tactile (premium feel), low friction, antimicrobial. Gold-anodised aluminium: lighter, cheaper, coating can scratch to reveal silver beneath. For a door handle: brass is superior.

questions.question: [Thermoplastics and Thermosets] Explain the structural difference between thermoplastics and thermosets and how this affects their recyclability.
questions.correctAnswer: Thermoplastics have linear chains with weak intermolecular forces - heat overcomes these, chains slide apart (melt), cool and reform. Repeatable = recyclable. Thermosets have cross-links (covalent bonds) - once cured, permanent, cannot be undone by heating, so they char rather than melt.
questions.explanation: Thermoplastics have linear chains with weak intermolecular forces - heat overcomes these, chains slide apart (melt), cool and reform. Repeatable = recyclable. Thermosets have cross-links (covalent bonds) - once cured, permanent, cannot be undone by heating, so they char rather than melt.

questions.question: [Thermoplastics and Thermosets] A designer needs a transparent, impact-resistant material for a safety goggles lens. Justify the choice of polycarbonate over acrylic.
questions.correctAnswer: Polycarbonate: extremely high impact resistance (250x stronger than glass, 30x stronger than acrylic), transparent. Acrylic: good transparency, but brittle - shatters on high impact. For safety goggles, polycarbonate is essential because it deforms rather than shatters.
questions.explanation: Polycarbonate: extremely high impact resistance (250x stronger than glass, 30x stronger than acrylic), transparent. Acrylic: good transparency, but brittle - shatters on high impact. For safety goggles, polycarbonate is essential because it deforms rather than shatters.

questions.question: [Thermoplastics and Thermosets] Explain why a living hinge on a shampoo bottle cap must be made from polypropylene and not from acrylic.
questions.correctAnswer: A living hinge is an extremely thin section that flexes repeatedly. Polypropylene has exceptional fatigue resistance - semi-crystalline structure allows millions of flex cycles. Acrylic is amorphous and brittle - would crack after very few flexes.
questions.explanation: A living hinge is an extremely thin section that flexes repeatedly. Polypropylene has exceptional fatigue resistance - semi-crystalline structure allows millions of flex cycles. Acrylic is amorphous and brittle - would crack after very few flexes.

questions.question: [Textiles and Fibres] Explain why polycotton is used for school shirts instead of 100% cotton or 100% polyester.
questions.correctAnswer: 100% cotton: comfortable but creases badly, shrinks. 100% polyester: durable and wrinkle-free but feels clammy, does not breathe. Polycotton (typically 65/35): retains cotton's breathability, gains polyester's durability and crease resistance, ideal for school uniforms.
questions.explanation: 100% cotton: comfortable but creases badly, shrinks. 100% polyester: durable and wrinkle-free but feels clammy, does not breathe. Polycotton (typically 65/35): retains cotton's breathability, gains polyester's durability and crease resistance, ideal for school uniforms.

questions.question: [Textiles and Fibres] Compare woven and knitted fabric constructions, explaining why each suits different garments.
questions.correctAnswer: Woven: warp + weft at 90 degrees, stable, holds shape - suits structured garments (shirts, trousers). Knitted: interlocking loops, stretchy, comfortable - suits body-hugging garments (t-shirts, socks, sportswear).
questions.explanation: Woven: warp + weft at 90 degrees, stable, holds shape - suits structured garments (shirts, trousers). Knitted: interlocking loops, stretchy, comfortable - suits body-hugging garments (t-shirts, socks, sportswear).

questions.question: [Textiles and Fibres] Discuss the environmental impact of synthetic fibres compared to natural fibres.
questions.correctAnswer: Synthetic: petrochemicals (non-renewable), microplastic shedding, non-biodegradable, but durable and recyclable. Natural: renewable, biodegradable, but cotton needs vast water and pesticides. Neither is perfectly sustainable - blended fabrics are hardest to recycle.
questions.explanation: Synthetic: petrochemicals (non-renewable), microplastic shedding, non-biodegradable, but durable and recyclable. Natural: renewable, biodegradable, but cotton needs vast water and pesticides. Neither is perfectly sustainable - blended fabrics are hardest to recycle.
